samples.text:
Nowadays, traffic congestion is becoming a big problem in many towns and cities around the world. This essay will discuss the problems that traffic jams cause and some solutions to solve them.

One of the main problem is that people waste a lot of time. Many workers spend one or two hours in their car every day, and this make them tired and stressed before they even start working. Also, when goods cannot be delivered on time, companies lose money, so it is bad for the economy too. Another serious problem is pollution. When many cars are stuck in traffic, their engines are still running and they produce a lot of smoke. This smoke is harmful for people who live near busy roads, especially children and old people, and it can cause breathing problems.

There are some ways to solve these problems. Firstly, the government should improve public transport. If buses and trains are cheap, fast and comfortable, many people will leave their cars at home. Secondly, cities can build more cycle lanes, so people can go to work by bicycle safely. This is also good for their health. Thirdly, some cities make drivers to pay money when they drive into the city centre at busy times. I think this is a good idea because it reduce the number of cars on the road. Finally, companies can let their employees to work from home some days of the week.

In conclusion, traffic congestion waste people's time, damages the economy and causes pollution. However, if governments and companies take the right actions, like better public transport and charges for drivers, this problem can be solved.
samples.why: Problems and solutions both covered · several solutions listed with little explanation · mechanical linking (Firstly to Finally) · adequate vocabulary with some repetition · verb pattern and agreement errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Traffic congestion has become a daily reality in many towns and cities, as the number of vehicles on the roads continues to grow faster than the capacity of the road network. This essay will discuss the main problems caused by congestion and propose some practical solutions.

Firstly, congestion has significant economic costs. Commuters lose hours each week sitting in traffic, which reduces the time they have for work, family and rest, and delayed delivery vehicles increase costs for businesses, which are eventually passed on to consumers. Secondly, and perhaps more seriously, heavy traffic damages the environment and public health. Vehicles moving slowly or idling in queues release large amounts of exhaust fumes, contributing to poor air quality in city centres and to respiratory illnesses such as asthma. The noise and stress associated with constant traffic also lowers the quality of life for people who live along busy roads.

There are several ways in which these problems could be tackled. The most effective long-term solution is to invest in reliable, affordable public transport, so that taking the bus or train becomes a more attractive option than driving. Cities which have developed efficient metro and tram systems generally have fewer cars on their streets. Alongside this, authorities could introduce congestion charges, which require drivers to pay to enter the busiest areas at peak times. This not only discourages unnecessary journeys but also raises money that can be reinvested in transport. Finally, encouraging cycling and walking through safe, separated lanes and pedestrian-friendly streets would provide a healthy alternative for shorter journeys.

In conclusion, traffic congestion wastes time and money and harms both the environment and people's health. A combination of better public transport, congestion charging and support for cycling offers the most realistic way to reduce it.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · economic and health problems extended and supported · solutions explained with reasons · wide range of linking, slightly formulaic (Firstly, Secondly) · good collocation · one agreement slip.

samples.text:
As car ownership has risen, the road networks of many towns and cities have become chronically congested, with rush-hour gridlock now an accepted part of urban life. This situation carries substantial economic, environmental and social costs, yet it is far from inevitable, and a number of well-tested measures can relieve it.

The economic burden of congestion is considerable. Time spent stationary in traffic is time lost to productive work or leisure, and unpredictable journey times make it harder for businesses to schedule deliveries and for employees to arrive punctually. These inefficiencies ripple through the economy, raising costs for firms and ultimately for consumers. The environmental and health consequences are equally serious. Stop-start driving is particularly inefficient, so congested streets generate disproportionate levels of exhaust emissions, degrading air quality and contributing to respiratory and heart disease. Residents of busy corridors also endure persistent noise, while heavy traffic discourages walking and cycling, reinforcing sedentary lifestyles.

Expanding road capacity might appear to be the obvious answer, but new roads tend to attract additional traffic and soon fill up again. A more effective strategy is to reduce demand for car travel. Frequent, affordable and reliable public transport is central to this, since people will only abandon their cars if a genuine alternative exists. Congestion charging, under which drivers pay to enter central zones at peak times, can then discourage non-essential journeys while generating revenue to fund transport improvements. Cities can further reshape travel habits by building safe, segregated cycle routes and by encouraging employers to adopt flexible hours and remote working, which spreads demand more evenly across the day.

In conclusion, congestion wastes time, burdens the economy and damages public health. Rather than building ever more roads, authorities should reduce reliance on cars through high-quality public transport, pricing mechanisms and support for active travel.
samples.why: Fully addresses problems and solutions with well-developed arguments · evaluates an obvious solution before proposing better ones · skilful cohesion · precise, natural vocabulary (ripple through, segregated cycle routes) · wide range of error-free structures.
